articles.title: Coordinated action on clean air and climate change can net $15 for every dollar spent
articles.summary: Tackling air pollution and climate change together can save millions of lives, reduce global warming and generate roughly $15 in economic benefits for every $1 spent, a new UN-backed report has revealed.
articles.content:
The assessment by the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) and the Climate and Clean Air Coalition (CCAC) shows how coordinated action can improve public health, strengthen economies and accelerate progress on climate goals through 25 proven measures and policy reforms.

These include using renewable energy, electric vehicles and clean fuel sources for cooking.

It comes as the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) also underlined the importance of coordinated action as increased pollution from wildfires and heatwaves threatens to undermine global efforts to improve air quality,

Tweet URL

Making the case

The report finds that combining efforts produces higher returns than addressing climate change and air pollution separately, because many of the same sectors and pollutants drive both crises.

“For too long, we have treated climate action as a cost to be managed and air pollution as the unfortunate outcome of development,” said Inger Andersen, Executive Director of UNEP.

“This report shows the opposite: clean air is a key driver of development, health, food and energy security, and climate stability – an asset we must invest in.”

The report – Hidden assets: The economic and health case for climate and clean air action – was released on the International Day of Clean Air for blue skies, observed annually on 7 September.

“The case for action has never been clearer,” UN Secretary-General António Guterres said in his message.

“Reducing air pollution protects health, boosts productivity, and builds more resilient and prosperous societies,” while “accelerating the transition away from fossil fuels is one of the fastest and most effective ways to clean the air while tackling the climate crisis.”

Benefits of investing

The report estimates that annual benefits from implementing the 25 measures would be equivalent to 2.8 per cent of global gross domestic product (GDP) in 2035, 4.5 per cent in 2050 and 11.4 per cent in 2100.

By comparison, explicit fossil fuel subsidies accounted for 2.18 per cent of global GDP in 2022, while healthcare spending reached 9.3 per cent in 2023.

Even when non-market welfare gains are excluded, such as the value of longer and healthier lives, the measures still return around $4 for every dollar invested.

Elliott Harris, independent co-chair of the assessment, said the findings should change how finance ministries and investors view clean-air policies.

“A benefit-cost ratio of 15 to 1 would attract capital instantly in almost any other sector,” he said. “Every year of delay costs the world more than $1.5 trillion in benefits we will not get back.”

A heavy toll on health

The health stakes are severe. The report estimates that in 2025, exposure to human-caused outdoor air pollution, including fine particulate matter (PM2.5) and ozone, was linked to 6.4 million premature deaths worldwide.

Household air pollution was linked to a further two million premature deaths, including around 300,000 children.

The report also examines the wider economic burden of illness. In 2025, outdoor air pollution contributed to 5.5 million new cases of childhood asthma, two million new cases of dementia and millions of cases of heart attack, pulmonary disease, diabetes, stroke and lung cancer.

By 2050, full implementation of the 25 measures could cumulatively prevent 144 million air-pollution-related premature deaths, including 96 million from ambient air pollution alone, as well as hundreds of millions of cases of chronic disease.

Rapid returns

The package of measures spans six sectors: energy and fossil fuel systems, industry, transport, agriculture and food systems, residential cooking and heating, and waste management.

Measures include renewable power, energy efficiency, clean cooking and heating, stronger vehicle emission and efficiency standards, electric vehicles, low-sulfur shipping fuels, reduced oil and gas leaks, improved livestock and manure management, and more efficient fertilizer use.

Many of these actions would also curb so-called super pollutants, including methane, black carbon and hydrofluorocarbons, which have powerful near-term effects on the climate.

Immediate benefits

The climate benefits would be substantial. Compared with the report’s baseline scenario, immediate implementation would halve global carbon dioxide emissions by 2050, reduce methane emissions by 60 per cent and cut major air pollutants, including black carbon, sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, by around 70 per cent.

The measures would avoid approximately 0.34°C of global warming by 2050 and 1.4°C by the year 2100.

“When we modelled them together, the returns were larger than each could show alone,” said Simon Dietz, co-chair of the assessment and Professor of Environmental Policy at the London School of Economics.

The challenge now is implementation. The report identifies fragmented decision-making, limited enforcement capacity and weak government coordination as major barriers that could delay full action by almost eight years globally.

It calls for integrated climate, air-quality, health and economic planning, stronger institutions and enforcement, and better alignment of public and private finance.
articles.source: UN News - Global perspective Human stories

articles.title: Public asked to have their say on proposed new renewable energy company
articles.summary: The proposed plans aim to reduce the cost of energy in the long-term, but won't be able to set bills.
articles.content:
The company would not "replace existing energy suppliers or directly set household electricity prices", it said in a consultation document.

It added that its purpose would be to "help Wales reduce energy costs over time by developing and owning renewable energy assets" and "supporting local and community ownership, investing in smart local energy systems".

It would also "help more organisations use locally generated energy" and try to attract investment into Welsh energy infrastructure.

The company would be separate from Great British Energy, which the UK government set up in 2024.

TGC is working on a number of projects on land owned by the Welsh government, including proposed wind farms at Carreg Wen near Aberdare and Glyn Cothi in Carmarthenshire.

The consultation asks if TGC should form the basis of the new company and whether it should use its name or call itself Ynni Cymru, external.

It also proposes that the company could take stakes in larger schemes - suggesting this could involve offshore wind, marine energy and nuclear.

The consultation looks at establishing a Welsh Energy Wealth Fund to allow energy projects "to support the most vulnerable in Wales as well as those living in areas where projects are being delivered".

Speaking to BBC Radio Wales Breakfast, Price said: "Our vision for the future of the energy system in Wales is one in which it's clean, it's cheap and it's owned by us."

He said the organisation was bringing the different elements together "to create a single company that, if you like, has the range of expertise and the sort of critical mass of resources and knowledge to make a real difference".

Price said Wales was "an energy giant at the Industrial Revolution with coal, but unfortunately we didn't see the benefit of that being derived largely by our own people".

He added: "We don't want to make the same mistake with the huge potential that Wales has in this new energy revolution with renewable energy."

The minister said many of the levers for energy are decided at a UK level, but added that energy produced by a public energy company could allow "lower energy prices" through agreements with local large energy users.
articles.reasoning: The article describes a proposed new renewable energy company in Wales aimed at reducing energy costs long-term, supporting local and community ownership, and investing in renewable energy infrastructure. This initiative has broad significance for the public by promoting clean energy, potentially lowering energy prices, and supporting vulnerable populations. The article provides sufficient detail on the company's goals, projects, and consultation process, indicating a meaningful positive impact on society and the environment.

articles.title: Wildlife and access boost planned for city park
articles.summary: Coventry City Council will use developers' money to make the improvements to Longford Nature Park.
articles.content:
Work is due to start improving access and habitats for wildlife at a nature park in Coventry.

Longford Nature Park is a small reserve which the city council has designated as being of high importance to the city.

The improvements will include a new boardwalk across muddy parts of the park, litter-picking and the creation of shallow wetland habitats.

The work is being funded through Section 106 money, paid by developers to councils for major development projects in the area.

Councillor Patricia Hetherton said the improvements would help protect the biodiversity already at the park and make it easier for people to get closer to nature.

"Green spaces like Longford Park play an important role in supporting our health and wellbeing," she added.
articles.reasoning: The article describes a local government initiative to enhance a nature park by improving wildlife habitats and public access, funded by developer contributions. This represents a tangible positive environmental impact with benefits for biodiversity and community wellbeing, addressing conservation and public engagement with nature.

articles.title: Study to reveal more about Guernsey's wild ferrets
articles.summary: A conservation group has been spending a year studying wild ferrets after securing government funds.
articles.content:
The results of a year-long research project are expected to reveal more about Guernsey's wild ferret population than ever, project leaders have said.

Using money from the government's Strategy for Nature fund, La Société Guernesiaise has been tracking the animals by using specialist camera equipment.

The conservation charity said it plotted where devices should be located in areas where ferrets had been known to attack different wildlife, such as La Claire Mare Nature Reserve in St Peters, had taken thousands of photos and the pictures were now being examined.

La Société said it had been aware of the feral ferret population for some time, but "didn't know anything about them".

The charity was one of 11 local projects to be given funding from the Strategy for Nature last year, and applied for cash to buy 15 camera traps.

The traps were motion-activated and used to take photos or videos of wildlife and people without anyone having to be there to operate them, project leaders said.
articles.reasoning: The article describes a funded conservation project studying wild ferrets in Guernsey, which contributes to understanding and potentially protecting local wildlife. The project has government backing and uses technology to gather valuable ecological data, indicating a positive environmental impact with meaningful scope and sufficient detail.
articles.personality_title: New study sheds light on Guernsey’s wild ferrets

**Context** – Guernsey is home to a group of wild ferrets, but little is known about their habits and how they affect local wildlife. To learn more, a conservation group started a research project last year.

**What happened** – La Société Guernesiaise, a local conservation charity, received government funding to study ferrets in Guernsey. They used 15 special camera traps that take pictures or videos when they detect movement. These cameras were placed in areas where ferrets had been seen, such as the La Claire Mare Nature Reserve. Over a year, the cameras captured thousands of images, which are now being studied.

**Impact** – This research is important because it helps people understand wild ferrets better. Before, the charity knew the ferrets existed but had no detailed information about them. Now, with this data, they can learn how ferrets live, what they eat, and how they interact with other animals. This knowledge can help protect Guernsey’s nature and keep the balance in local ecosystems.

**What's next step** – The researchers will analyze the photos and videos to draw clear conclusions about the ferret population. Their findings may guide future actions, like protecting certain areas or managing the ferret population to support other wildlife.

**One-sentence takeaway** – A new government-funded study using camera traps is uncovering valuable information about Guernsey’s wild ferrets, helping conservation efforts in the region.
